analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for oil spill cleanup costs and legal damages.
analysis.headline: The bill to deny tax deductions for oil spill cleanup costs and damages was introduced in July 2010 with 18 cosponsors, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, a company responsible for an oil spill can deduct the costs of cleaning it up and the damages it owes under the Oil Pollution Act, just like an ordinary business expense. This bill would end that, making polluters bear the full after-tax cost of the harm they cause. It never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, ordinary taxpayers would gain because companies responsible for oil spills would no longer effectively share their cleanup and damage costs with the public through the tax code. Communities and ecosystems harmed by spills would benefit from a stronger financial incentive for companies to prevent them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Internal Revenue Code to add a new section denying any deduction for costs or damages for which a taxpayer is liable under section 1002 of the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 [S3].

Under the Oil Pollution Act, responsible parties must pay removal costs and damages for oil discharges; the bill would make those payments non-deductible, so companies could not reduce their tax bills by the amount they spend on spills [S2].
The change would apply to any liability arising after December 31, 2009 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies responsible for spills would pay higher after-tax costs for cleanup and damages, and would face stronger financial incentives to prevent spills. In principle, some of that cost could be passed to consumers through fuel prices, though spill liability is tied to accidents rather than routine operations.

drawbacks.text: Ending the deduction raises the after-tax cost of spill liability, and companies may pass some of that cost on to consumers through fuel and energy prices rather than absorbing it entirely.

The Oil Pollution Act's liability scheme was already designed to make polluters pay for removal costs and damages; critics could argue the tax code change duplicates an existing penalty structure rather than adding deterrence [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward: polluters would no longer treat court-ordered cleanup costs and damages as a deductible business expense, so the public would stop effectively co-funding spill consequences. The main cost is that energy companies may pass some added expense to consumers, but because the added cost only applies to parties actually liable for spills, it functions as a targeted price on negligence rather than a broad tax. The bill was narrow and had no hearings or refinements, so its practical design details were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Connolly introduced the bill on July 28, 2010, during the aftermath of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax law [S5].
Eighteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further activity: no committee vote, no report, no floor action, before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies liable for oil spills kept the ability to deduct their cleanup costs and damages from their taxes, leaving taxpayers to continue sharing that burden through foregone revenue. The Ways and Means Committee, which took no action, faced no pressure to change the rule.

for.name: Rep. Gerald E. Connolly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to deny tax deductions for oil spill removal costs and damages.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 18 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to deduct spill cleanup costs and legal damages under the Oil Pollution Act, raising the after-tax price of causing a spill. The industry's interest in keeping the deduction runs directly against taxpayers, who currently absorb part of the cost through foregone revenue.
